Neonatal Rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) weigh approximately 464 grams [Wwb = approximately 464 grams] at birth, a value that reflects the species’ moderately precocial developmental trajectory among Old World primates. This birth mass, recorded from captive colonies at the Caribbean Primate Research Center, positions the newborn as substantially heavier than the altricial young of many comparably sized mammals, yet lighter than the neonates of great apes. The wet weight at birth provides the foundation for a rapid phase of growth, as the suckling juvenile depends entirely on maternal milk for its nutritional requirements during the initial weeks of life. The pup, as the newborn is often termed in field contexts, exhibits a well-developed pelage and open eyes within hours of parturition, enabling early clinging behavior essential for transport and predator avoidance. Studies indicate that the relatively generous birth mass, combined with the energetic richness of macaque milk, supports a swift accumulation of body tissue, setting the stage for subsequent milestones such as weaning and independent foraging. This initial investment by the mother in a single offspring, typical of macaque reproductive strategy, is a key determinant of neonatal survival in both wild and captive settings.

The adult body mass of Macaca mulatta, known as the ultimate wet weight, reaches approximately 8235 grams [Wwi = approximately 8235 grams] in well-nourished individuals, a figure derived from longitudinal studies of captive populations at the Yerkes National Primate Research Center. This asymptotic mass reflects the culmination of somatic growth following the juvenile and sub-adult phases, during which the weaned juvenile transitions from milk dependency to a diet dominated by fruits, seeds, and occasional animal matter. The substantial difference between the 464 gram birth mass and the 8235 gram adult mass underscores a period of rapid tissue accretion, particularly during the first few years of life. Field surveys of free-ranging groups in northern India report adult males averaging slightly heavier than this captive-derived value, while females typically plateau at a somewhat lower mass, a pattern consistent with the species’ moderate sexual dimorphism. The ultimate wet weight is a critical parameter for understanding basal metabolic requirements, ranging from the daily energetic costs of tissue upkeep to the caloric demands of gestation and lactation in reproductively active adults.

Under the basal thermal conditions typical of this species, approximated at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], several key life-history timetables have been empirically quantified. The gestation period, the duration between internal fertilisation and parturition, lasts 165 days [tg = 165 days], a value consistent across captive breeding records at facilities such as the Wisconsin National Primate Research Center at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This relatively short gestation for a primate of this body size is followed by a prolonged period of maternal investment. The time since birth at weaning, marking the cessation of lactation and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs at 292 days after birth [tx = 292 days after birth], at which point the juvenile weighs about 1454 grams [Wwx = about 1454 grams] at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This wet weight at weaning, representing a threefold increase from the birth mass, signals the successful transition from a milk-based diet to solid food foraging. The weaning mass is a critical threshold, as juveniles that fail to achieve this body condition often exhibit reduced survival rates during the subsequent dry season in wild populations.

Sexual maturation in Macaca mulatta, defined by the onset of puberty and the first appearance of gametogenesis, is attained at 1231 days after birth [tp = 1231 days after birth], a milestone measured under stable captive conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This period, spanning over three years, reflects the extended developmental delay characteristic of a large-brained, socially complex primate. During this juvenile and sub-adult phase, the individual progresses through a hierarchy of social learning, mastering foraging techniques, dominance interactions, and mating strategies before reaching reproductive viability. The wet weight of 1454 grams [Wwx = 1454 grams] at weaning is nearly achieved by the time of puberty, as the growing animal approaches the adult asymptotic mass of 8235 grams [Wwi = 8235 grams]. However, actual first reproduction typically occurs several months to a year after the onset of puberty, as females require time to establish stable social rank and males must compete for access to receptive partners. This temporal lag between physiological maturity and first breeding is common among cercopithecine primates.

The maximum lifespan documented for the Rhesus macaque, under optimal captive conditions and at a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], is approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years], a figure corroborated by longevity records from the Yerkes National Primate Research Center and the California National Primate Research Center. This extended lifespan, unusual among mammals of this body size, aligns with the species’ slow life-history pace, characterized by a long juvenile period, single offspring births, and extended maternal care. At the opposite end of the life-history continuum, the maximum reproductive rate has been assessed under controlled colony conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. Female macaques typically produce a single offspring per birth event [N_R_i = single offspring per birth event], and under optimal provisioning may give birth to one infant each year [Ri = one infant each year], yielding a modest lifetime reproductive output. The total body length from snout to tail tip in full-grown adults is 54 centimeters [Li = 54 centimeters], though field measurements of free-ranging troops in India and Nepal report a range of 45 to 64 cen(45-64 cm [Li = 45-64 cm]) timeters, reflecting geographic variation across the species’ vast distribution from Afghanistan to southern China.
